reconcile.connective: JFB reargues the Greek pronouns so the Lord's servant, not Satan, takes captive, and God's will, not Satan's, is obeyed.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible juxtaposes the two verses as a flat "Yes" vs. "No" on whether the devil can seize people at will.

excerpts.excerpt_text: taken captive by him at his will--so as to follow the will of "THAT" (the Greek emphatically marks Satan thus) foe. However, different Greek pronouns stand for "him" and "his"; and the Greek for "taken captive" means not "captured for destruction," but "for being saved alive," as in Luk 5:10, "Thou shalt catch men to save them unto life"; also there is no article before the Greek participle, which the English Version "who are taken captive," would require. Therefore, translate, "That they may awake . . . taken as saved (and willing) captives by him (the servant of the Lord, Ti2 2:24), so as to follow the will of HIM (the Lord, Ti2 2:24, or "God," Ti2 2:25)."
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB reinterprets the Greek antecedents in 'taken captive by him at his will' so the captor is the Lord's servant and the will followed is God's, not Satan's — directly undercutting the premise that the devil captures people at his own arbitrary discretion, which is what the contradiction depends on.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871)
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats this exact passage directly, arguing from the Greek that the captives of 2 Timothy 2:26 are willingly won to God's will rather than seized at Satan's own arbitrary will, which would otherwise stand against James 4:7's easy resistibility.
